jsnvu6-e183663-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 2 of d.25: whether the articles are fittingly set out in the Creed, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e122.summary: Argument against the Creed: Scripture is the rule of faith, to which nothing may be added or taken away (Deut. 4); so the articles should not be contained in another writing, and making a creed as a rule of faith was not permitted.
claims: Nothing may be added to Scripture, so a creed as rule of faith is illicit (objection)

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e144.summary: Second argument: there is one Lord and one faith (Eph. 4), so the rule of faith should be one, and positing three creeds—Apostles', Nicene, Athanasian—is wrong.
claims: Three creeds contradict the unity of faith (objection)

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e158.summary: Argument for the opposite: the universal Church cannot err, being ruled by the Spirit of truth (John 16), and the Creed was composed by the Church's authority.
claims: The Creed is legitimate because composed by the inerrant Church

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e171.summary: Outline of the response: what an article is; what a creed is and why it was composed; and the distinction of the articles in the Creed.

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e184.summary: An article, per Richard of St Victor, is an indivisible truth about God constraining us to believe. Indivisible not as incomplex—truth belongs to complexes—but as not resolvable into several truths with special difficulties, like a bodily joint (a finger, not the hand). Since faith concerns what exceeds nature, each article has its own difficulty; what easily follows from or accompanies an article, like Christ's burial following his death, does not make a new article.
claims: An article is an indivisible truth about God constraining belief
Indivisibility means not resolvable into truths with distinct difficulties
What follows easily from an article is not a separate article

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e232.summary: 'Constraining us to believe' means necessity of supposition—if we wish to be saved—not coercion, since no one believes unwillingly. 'Article' may mean what faith constrains us to believe, including demonstrable truths like God's unity, creation, and omnipotence, or, strictly and properly, only what faith alone constrains us to believe, exceeding the wayfarer's natural reason, like the Trinity and the Incarnation.
claims: Faith constrains belief by necessity of supposition, not coercion
Strictly, articles of faith are only truths exceeding natural reason
Demonstrable truths like God's unity are articles only in a broad sense

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e265.summary: 'Symbolum' derives from gathering, as when several contribute to one banquet: a gathering of many people into one faith, of preachers declaring it, and of articles drawn from various parts of Scripture. It serves two uses: certain and easier knowledge of what must be believed, and protection against heretics. Since the truths of faith are scattered and obscure in Scripture, requiring long study impossible for all who need them, it was necessary to collect them summarily so the faith of the simple would not be corrupted.
claims: 'Symbolum' signifies a collection
The Creed provides easier knowledge of credibles and protection against heresy
The Creed summarizes truths scattered and obscure in Scripture for the simple

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e309.summary: Three creeds: the Apostles' Creed, composed before truth was proclaimed and so said quietly; the Nicene, for proclaiming truth against heretics, sung after the Gospel at solemn Mass, elucidating difficult points of the Apostles' Creed; and the Athanasian, issued when truth was shaken by heretics but prevailing, said at dawn, more a doctrine than a creed. All contain the same truth, more or less explicitly according to the heresies of different times.
claims: The three creeds contain the same truth with different degrees of explicitness
Creeds were developed in response to heresies arising at different times

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e351.summary: Distinction of the articles: articles concern either the majesty of the divinity or the mystery of the assumed humanity. Divinity: unity (I believe in God); trinity, with three articles for Father, Son, and Spirit; and divine works, with three articles for nature (Creator), grace (Church, communion, remission), and glory (resurrection, eternal life). Humanity: seven—conception, birth, passion, descent into hell, resurrection, ascension, coming to judgment. The alternative of assigning articles by the number of apostles is rejected as accidental and less artful.
claims: The articles divide into seven on the divinity and seven on Christ's humanity
Assigning articles by the twelve apostles is accidental and less artful
concepts: works of nature, grace, and glory

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e414.summary: Reply to the first argument: nothing may be added to Scripture that is dissonant with it, diminishing or corrupting it, but what further declares it may well be added (Sirach 24: those who elucidate me shall have eternal life). Excerpting and collecting what is scattered in Scripture and most necessary for belief, for instruction of the simple and against heretics, is useful, as the Creed does.
claims: Additions that elucidate Scripture without contradicting it are licit
The Creed collects scattered scriptural truths

jsnvu6-e183663-d1e440.summary: Reply to the second: the three creeds contain one truth, more explicit in one than another because of new heresies, and plurality in words with unity in substance does not conflict with the unity of faith.
claims: Plurality of creeds in words is compatible with unity of faith in substance

jsnvu6-e183663.summary: Question 2 of d.25 asks whether the articles are fittingly set out in the Creed, against objections that nothing may be added to Scripture and that one faith requires one creed. Durandus defines an article, following Richard of St Victor, as an indivisible truth about God constraining belief. It is indivisible because it cannot be resolved into truths with distinct difficulties: Christ's burial goes with his death. It constrains by necessity of supposition, not by coercion. Strictly, only truths exceeding natural reason, such as the Trinity and the Incarnation, are articles; demonstrable truths are articles only broadly. 'Symbolum' means a collection, and the Creed gathers truths scattered and obscure in Scripture so that the simple can know them easily and are protected from heresy. The Apostles', Nicene, and Athanasian creeds contain one truth, made more explicit as heresies arose. The articles are distinguished as seven on the divinity (unity, three persons, works of nature, grace, and glory) and seven on Christ's humanity; the scheme based on the twelve apostles is rejected as accidental. Elucidating Scripture is licit, and plurality of creeds in words is compatible with unity of faith in substance.
claims: An article is an indivisible truth about God, involving a distinct difficulty, constraining belief for salvation
Strictly, articles are only truths exceeding natural reason
The Creed licitly collects scattered scriptural truths for the simple and against heretics
The three creeds express one faith with varying explicitness
There are fourteen articles, seven on the divinity and seven on the humanity
